en.title: Industrial Chemistry: the whole course
en.short: What industrial chemistry covers, how the degree is organised, and how to study it well.

sections.heading: What industrial chemistry is
sections.text:
Industrial chemistry is the study of how chemical knowledge is turned into products at commercial scale. It covers choosing reactions, designing and operating processes, controlling quality, and managing safety, waste and cost. It sits between pure chemistry and chemical engineering, and borrows from both.

A pure chemist asks whether a reaction works and what it makes. An industrial chemist asks a harder set of questions: can it be run safely, at large scale, with consistent quality, without damaging people or the environment, and at a price the market will pay? That is why the course mixes chemistry with balances, equipment, economics and regulation.

These summaries teach principles. They do not replace a plant’s operating procedures, a safety data sheet, a national standard or the law of your country. Real processes must follow the current regulations where they operate, and those regulations differ from country to country.

sections.heading: How the degree is usually organised
sections.text:
Length and awards differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook rather than relying on a general description. In Nigeria, a BSc in Industrial Chemistry commonly takes four years, and students normally spend a period in industry under SIWES, the Students Industrial Work Experience Scheme. Polytechnics usually offer an ND and then an HND, each commonly two years, in chemistry, polymer technology or a related field. In the United Kingdom a BSc usually takes three years and an MChem four. Other countries follow their own patterns.

The early years are shared with other chemistry students: mathematics, physics, general, organic, inorganic, physical and analytical chemistry, and laboratory work. Later years add process subjects, product-based subjects, quality control, economics, safety and environmental management. Most programmes end with a project or dissertation.

A master’s degree adds advanced reaction engineering, modelling and simulation, advanced materials, and research methods leading to a dissertation. Professional bodies also differ: Nigeria has the Chemical Society of Nigeria and the Institute of Chartered Chemists of Nigeria, while the United Kingdom has the Royal Society of Chemistry. Check which body regulates practice in your country.

sections.heading: The foundation areas
sections.text:
The intro stage builds the chemistry and the mathematical tools you will use all the way through. Mathematics for industrial chemistry covers units and dimensions, graphs, and the calculus used for rates and optimisation. Atomic structure and bonding, including intermolecular forces, explain why substances behave as they do.

Stoichiometry and chemical calculations come next, and they must become automatic. Organic chemistry introduces functional groups and their reactions. Inorganic chemistry covers periodic trends and coordination compounds. Physical chemistry covers thermodynamics and equilibrium, which later become the basis of process energy calculations.

Analytical chemistry teaches measurement: how to take a sample, calibrate an instrument and state an uncertainty. Laboratory safety and chemical hygiene belong here too, not at the end, because you will be in a laboratory from the first weeks.

sections.heading: The core stage
sections.text:
The core stage starts with material and energy balances, the backbone of all process work. Unit operations then cover mass and heat transfer: distillation, absorption, extraction, drying, evaporation and heat exchangers. Chemical thermodynamics for processes applies equilibrium ideas to real mixtures, and reaction kinetics and reactor design turn rate equations into vessel sizes.

Industrial catalysis follows, since most large processes depend on it. Process control and instrumentation, process economics and project evaluation, plant safety and risk management, and environmental management and green chemistry complete the process side.

The product side covers heavy inorganic chemicals and fertilisers, petrochemicals and refining, polymers and polymerisation, surfactants, soaps and detergents, cement, ceramics and glass, corrosion and materials selection, fine chemicals and pharmaceuticals, quality control and industrial analysis, and professional practice, ethics and regulation. At master’s level come advanced reaction engineering, process modelling and simulation, advanced materials and nanotechnology, and research methods with a dissertation.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Practise balances until they are routine. Draw a flowsheet, label every stream, choose a basis, then check that every element balance and the energy balance close. Most process problems are balances in disguise.

Write units on every line of every calculation, and ask whether the answer is physically sensible. Learn typical values, such as the approximate composition of air, so that a wrong answer stands out.

Keep a laboratory notebook as if it were a legal record, because in industry it often is. Read safety data sheets properly. For each product you study, link it to its raw materials, its main reaction, its separation steps and its main waste stream. That habit turns a list of industries into a connected picture.

sections.heading: Common mistakes

keyPoints: Industrial chemistry turns chemical knowledge into safe, consistent, profitable products at scale.
Degree length and awards differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook.
Material and energy balances are the backbone of every process calculation.
Write units on every line and check that each balance closes.
Link every product to its raw materials, reaction, separation steps and waste streams.
Safety, environmental law and economics are part of the chemistry, not extras.

en.title: Mathematics for industrial chemistry: units, graphs and calculus
en.short: SI units, dimensional analysis, significant figures, logs, graphs, and calculus for rates and areas.

sections.heading: Units and error
sections.text:
SI has seven base units: metre, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin, mole and candela. Derived units are built from them; the joule is kg m² s⁻². Dimensional analysis means writing a quantity as powers of the base units and checking that both sides of an equation match. For v = √(2gh), the right side has m² s⁻² under the root, giving m s⁻¹, the unit of v.

Significant figures are the digits that carry meaning: 0.0205 has three. When multiplying, keep the smallest number of significant figures among the inputs.

Error is given as absolute error (same units as the value) or relative error = absolute error ÷ true value, often as a percentage.

sections.heading: Logs and graphs
sections.text:
Logarithms turn products into sums: log(ab) = log a + log b, and ln means log to base e. The exponential y = y₀e^(−kt) becomes a straight line when ln y is plotted against t, with slope −k and intercept ln y₀. Chemists plot data this way to test a model.

On a straight-line graph, slope = Δy ÷ Δx and the intercept is where the line crosses the y-axis. Label each axis with quantity and unit.

sections.heading: Calculus for rates
sections.text:
A derivative is an instantaneous rate. If concentration c falls with time, dc/dt is the rate of change, negative for a reactant. For c = atⁿ, dc/dt = nat^(n−1); the derivative of a constant is zero. Integration reverses differentiation and gives the area under a curve, so ∫(dc/dt)dt = c₂ − c₁.

Example: c = 0.500 − 0.040t + 0.0010t² (mol dm⁻³, t in s).
dc/dt = −0.040 + 0.0020t
At t = 10 s: −0.040 + 0.020 = −0.020 mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹
Change in c from 0 to 10 s = −0.040(10) + 0.0010(10²) = −0.400 + 0.100 = −0.300 mol dm⁻³
Check: c(10) = 0.500 − 0.400 + 0.100 = 0.200, and 0.200 − 0.500 = −0.300.

keyPoints: SI base units are metre, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin, mole and candela; check equations by their dimensions.
Relative error = absolute error ÷ true value; keep significant figures consistent with the inputs.
ln y = ln y₀ − kt gives a straight line of slope −k for exponential decay.
Slope of a graph = Δy ÷ Δx; the intercept is where the line crosses the y-axis.
For c = atⁿ, dc/dt = nat^(n−1); the derivative of a constant is zero.
Integration gives the area under a curve: ∫(dc/dt)dt = c₂ − c₁.

en.title: Atomic structure, bonding and intermolecular forces
en.short: Electron arrangements, periodic trends, bonding types, molecular shape and forces behind properties.

sections.heading: Electronic structure
sections.text:
An atom has a nucleus of protons and neutrons, surrounded by electrons. Electrons occupy shells and subshells (s, p, d, f) of increasing energy. The electron configuration lists this arrangement; sodium is 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s¹. The outermost electrons are valence electrons, and they control bonding and reactivity.

Across a period, atomic radius generally falls and ionisation energy (energy needed to remove an electron) generally rises. Down a group, extra shells make atoms larger and ionisation energy generally falls. Electronegativity, an atom’s pull on shared electrons, follows the same pattern.

sections.heading: Bonding and shape
sections.text:
Ionic bonding is the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions, formed when one atom transfers electrons to another, as in sodium chloride. Covalent bonding is a shared pair of electrons, as in hydrogen or a carbon-hydrogen bond. A polar covalent bond has unequal sharing because the atoms differ in electronegativity. Metallic bonding is a lattice of positive metal ions held together by delocalised electrons, which explains conduction and malleability.

Molecular shape follows VSEPR theory: electron pairs around a central atom repel and arrange as far apart as possible. Lone pairs repel more strongly, giving linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, trigonal pyramidal and bent shapes.

sections.heading: Forces and properties
sections.text:
Molecules attract by intermolecular forces: London dispersion forces (temporary dipoles), dipole-dipole attraction between polar molecules, and hydrogen bonding, a strong attraction when hydrogen is bonded to N, O or F. These forces are weaker than covalent bonds but decide boiling point and solubility. Boiling point rises as intermolecular forces become stronger or molecules become larger, because more energy is needed to separate particles. Solubility follows like-dissolves-like: polar and ionic substances dissolve in polar solvents such as water; nonpolar substances dissolve in nonpolar solvents such as hexane.

Case: Amina finds that table salt dissolves in water but not kerosene, while cooking oil does the reverse. Reactivity follows valence electrons: metals tend to lose electrons, nonmetals gain or share them, and noble gases with full shells are usually unreactive.

keyPoints: Electron configuration shows how electrons fill shells and subshells, and valence electrons control bonding.
Atomic radius generally falls across a period and rises down a group; ionisation energy and electronegativity show the opposite general trend.
Ionic bonds transfer electrons, covalent bonds share electrons, and metallic bonds use delocalised electrons.
VSEPR explains molecular shape from electron-pair repulsion, with lone pairs repelling more strongly.
Intermolecular forces are weaker than covalent bonds but set boiling point and solubility.
Like dissolves like: polar and ionic substances prefer polar solvents, while nonpolar substances prefer nonpolar solvents.

en.title: Stoichiometry and chemical calculations
en.short: Moles, formulae, balancing, limiting reagents, yield, concentration, dilution and titration calculations.

sections.heading: Moles and formulae
sections.text: The mole is the amount of substance containing 6.022 × 10²³ entities (Avogadro constant). One mole of an element or compound has a mass in grams equal to its relative atomic, molecular or formula mass, called the molar mass M (g/mol). So n = m ÷ M. The empirical formula is the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms; the molecular formula is the actual number, found from molar mass ÷ empirical formula mass. For example, CH2 has empirical mass 14 g/mol; if M = 42 g/mol, the molecular formula is C3H6.

sections.heading: Equations and limiting reagent
sections.text: Balance equations by changing coefficients only, so atoms and charge are conserved. The coefficients give mole ratios. The limiting reagent is the reactant used up first; it sets the maximum product. Calculate moles of each reactant, divide by its coefficient, and the smallest result is limiting. Example: 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O. 3.0 g H2 = 1.5 mol; 16 g O2 = 0.5 mol. O2 needs 1.0 mol H2, so O2 is limiting and gives 1.0 mol H2O, mass 18 g. If 15 g is obtained, percentage yield = 15 ÷ 18 × 100 = 83.3%.

sections.heading: Concentration and dilution
sections.text: Concentration c = n ÷ V, with V in dm³ (1 dm³ = 1000 cm³). Molarity is mol/dm³. Mass concentration is mass ÷ volume, often g/dm³. Dilution conserves moles: c1V1 = c2V2. Example: 0.10 mol NaCl in 250 cm³ gives c = 0.10 ÷ 0.250 = 0.40 mol/dm³. Diluting 25.0 cm³ of this to 250 cm³ gives c2 = 0.40 × 25.0 ÷ 250 = 0.040 mol/dm³.

sections.heading: Volumetric calculations
sections.text: In a titration, moles react in the ratio shown by the balanced equation. At equivalence, n(acid) ÷ n(base) equals the coefficient ratio. Example: 25.0 cm³ of 0.10 mol/dm³ NaOH neutralises 20.0 cm³ HCl in a 1:1 reaction. n(NaOH) = 0.10 × 0.0250 = 0.00250 mol, so c(HCl) = 0.00250 ÷ 0.0200 = 0.125 mol/dm³.

keyPoints: n = m ÷ M, and one mole contains 6.022 × 10²³ entities.
Empirical formula is the simplest ratio; molecular formula = empirical formula × (molar mass ÷ empirical formula mass).
Balance equations with coefficients; the limiting reagent sets the theoretical yield.
Percentage yield = actual yield ÷ theoretical yield × 100.
c = n ÷ V with V in dm³; dilution follows c1V1 = c2V2.
In titrations, use the balanced equation mole ratio with c = n ÷ V.

en.title: Organic chemistry: functional groups and reactions
en.short: Naming, structure, isomerism and main reactions of the common organic functional groups.

sections.heading: Naming and isomerism
sections.text:
Organic compounds are named by IUPAC rules: find the longest carbon chain, number to give lowest locants to substituents and the principal group, then add the suffix. Suffixes include -ane, -ene, -yne, -ol, -al, -one, -oic acid and -amine. A functional group is an atom or group that gives a family its characteristic reactions.

Isomers have the same molecular formula but different structures. Structural isomers differ in chain, position or functional group. Stereoisomers differ only in spatial arrangement, such as cis-trans in alkenes.

Example: C4H10 is butane, CH3CH2CH2CH3, or 2-methylpropane, (CH3)3CH; both have four carbons but different boiling points.

sections.heading: Hydrocarbons
sections.text:
Alkanes are saturated, CnH2n+2, and mostly undergo free-radical substitution with halogens under UV light. Alkenes have C=C, CnH2n, and alkynes have C≡C, CnH2n−2; both are unsaturated and undergo addition, for example ethene plus H2 over nickel gives ethane.

Benzene, C6H6, is aromatic: planar, with delocalised π electrons, unusually stable, and it reacts mainly by electrophilic substitution such as nitration to nitrobenzene.

sections.heading: Oxygen and nitrogen groups
sections.text:
Alcohols contain -OH. Primary alcohols can be oxidised to aldehydes and then to carboxylic acids; secondary alcohols oxidise to ketones. Carbonyl compounds contain C=O: aldehydes RCHO and ketones RCOR'. Carboxylic acids RCOOH are acidic and form esters with alcohols. Amines RNH2 are basic and can be made by reducing nitriles or nitro compounds.

Example: ethanol oxidised by acidified dichromate gives ethanoic acid; ethanol plus ethanoic acid with acid catalyst gives ethyl ethanoate and water.

sections.heading: Industrial reactions
sections.text: Industrial synthesis uses a few reaction types. Addition adds atoms across a double or triple bond, as in hydrogenation. Substitution replaces one atom or group, as in methane chlorination or aromatic nitration. Elimination removes atoms to form a multiple bond, as in ethanol dehydration to ethene. Oxidation and reduction change oxygen or hydrogen content. Esterification joins a carboxylic acid and an alcohol; amidation joins an acid derivative and an amine. Hydrolysis breaks esters, amides or nitriles with water. The functional group predicts which type is possible, so naming and structure guide route choice.

keyPoints: IUPAC names use the longest chain and lowest locants, with suffixes such as -ol, -al, -one, -oic acid and -amine.
Isomers share a molecular formula but differ in structure or spatial arrangement.
Alkanes are saturated and react by free-radical substitution; alkenes and alkynes are unsaturated and react by addition.
Benzene is aromatic and reacts mainly by electrophilic substitution.
Primary alcohols oxidise to aldehydes then carboxylic acids; secondary alcohols oxidise to ketones.
Industrial routes use addition, substitution, elimination, oxidation, reduction, esterification, amidation and hydrolysis.

en.title: Inorganic chemistry: periodic trends and coordination compounds
en.short: Periodic trends, oxidation states, ligands, coordination compounds and simple crystal structures.

sections.heading: Periodic trends
sections.text: Across a period, atomic radius falls and ionisation energy and electronegativity rise; down a group the reverse happens. These trends follow effective nuclear charge and shielding. Main-group elements often have a characteristic oxidation state, and their oxides range from basic (sodium oxide) to acidic (sulfur trioxide). Transition metals have partly filled d orbitals, so they show several oxidation states and form coloured compounds. Industrial catalysts often use transition metals because d electrons can bind reactant molecules and weaken their bonds.

sections.heading: Oxidation states
sections.text: Oxidation state is the charge an atom would carry if bonding electrons were given to the more electronegative atom. In a neutral compound the oxidation states sum to zero; in an ion they sum to the ion charge. Fluorine is always −1 in compounds, oxygen is usually −2, and hydrogen is +1 with non-metals. Example: in K4[Fe(CN)6], potassium is +1 and cyanide is −1. Let x be iron: 4(+1) + x + 6(−1) = 0, so x = +2. The complex ion is [Fe(CN)6]4−.

sections.heading: Coordination compounds
sections.text: A coordination compound contains a central metal ion bonded to ligands. A ligand is an ion or molecule that donates an electron pair; the atom that donates is the donor atom. The coordination number is the number of donor atoms bonded to the metal. Common shapes are linear (2), tetrahedral (4), square planar (4) and octahedral (6). Ligands split the metal d orbitals into different energy levels. This crystal field splitting explains colour and magnetism. For example, [Fe(CN)6]4− is octahedral with six cyanide ligands; iron(II) has six d electrons, and strong-field cyanide leaves it low spin and diamagnetic.

sections.heading: Crystal structures
sections.text: Simple crystal structures describe how ions or atoms pack in a lattice. A unit cell is the repeating box. Face-centred cubic and hexagonal close-packed are common close packings. In sodium chloride each Na+ has six Cl− neighbours, giving 6:6 coordination; caesium chloride gives 8:8. These structures affect density, hardness and ionic conduction, and matter in ceramics and catalysts.

keyPoints: Across a period atomic radius falls while ionisation energy and electronegativity rise; down a group the reverse occurs.
Oxidation state is the charge left when bonding electrons are assigned to the more electronegative atom; in a neutral compound the states sum to zero.
In K4[Fe(CN)6], iron has oxidation state +2 because 4(+1) + x + 6(−1) = 0.
A ligand donates an electron pair to a metal ion; coordination number counts donor atoms.
Common coordination shapes are linear, tetrahedral, square planar and octahedral.
Crystal field splitting of d orbitals explains colour and magnetism in transition-metal complexes; NaCl has 6:6 and CsCl 8:8 coordination.

en.title: Physical chemistry: thermodynamics and equilibrium
en.short: First law, enthalpy, entropy, Gibbs energy, equilibrium and phase changes with simple calculations.

sections.heading: Energy and enthalpy
sections.text:
The first law says energy is conserved. For a closed system, ΔU = q + w, where ΔU is change in internal energy, q is heat added to the system and w is work done on it. With pressure-volume work, w = −pΔV at constant pressure. Check your course’s convention.

Enthalpy is H = U + pV. At constant pressure, heat exchanged equals ΔH. ΔH° refers to reactants and products in their standard states (1 bar for gases, 1 M for solutes). Exothermic reactions have ΔH < 0.

sections.heading: Entropy and Gibbs energy
sections.text:
Entropy S measures energy dispersal. For a reversible change at temperature T, ΔS = qrev ÷ T. The second law says ΔS_universe ≥ 0 for a spontaneous process. Gibbs energy is G = H − TS. At constant temperature and pressure, ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, and a process is spontaneous if ΔG < 0.

Example: ΔH = −50.0 kJ/mol and ΔS = −100 J/K/mol at 298 K.
ΔG = −50,000 − 298 × (−100) = −20,200 J/mol = −20.2 kJ/mol.
It becomes nonspontaneous above T = ΔH ÷ ΔS = 500 K.

sections.heading: Chemical equilibrium
sections.text:
At equilibrium, forward and reverse rates balance and composition stops changing. The equilibrium constant K is the reaction quotient Q at equilibrium; Q compares product terms with reactant terms. For gases, K uses partial pressures; for solutes, concentrations relative to a standard state. The standard Gibbs energy change is ΔG° = −RT ln K. A negative ΔG° means K > 1.

If Q < K the reaction moves forward; if Q > K it moves backward.

sections.heading: Phase changes
sections.text: At a phase transition, the two phases are in equilibrium, so ΔG = 0 and ΔH = TΔS. Thus the boiling point is T = ΔHvap ÷ ΔSvap. For water, ΔHvap is about 40.7 kJ/mol and ΔSvap is about 109 J/K/mol, giving T ≈ 373 K at 1 atm. Values vary slightly with pressure and data source. Phase diagrams show which phase is stable at a given temperature and pressure.

keyPoints: First law for a closed system: ΔU = q + w, with w = −pΔV for pressure-volume work at constant pressure (IUPAC convention).
Enthalpy is H = U + pV, and at constant pressure the heat exchanged is ΔH.
Entropy change for a reversible process is ΔS = qrev ÷ T; the second law requires ΔS_universe ≥ 0 for spontaneity.
Gibbs energy is G = H − TS, and at constant T and p a process is spontaneous when ΔG = ΔH − TΔS < 0.
At equilibrium ΔG = 0 for a phase change, so T = ΔH ÷ ΔS; for chemical equilibrium ΔG° = −RT ln K.
Compare Q with K: Q < K favours products and Q > K favours reactants.

en.title: Analytical chemistry: measurement and basic techniques
en.short: Sampling, calibration, volumetric and gravimetric analysis, titrations and basic spectroscopy.

sections.heading: Sampling and calibration
sections.text: Sampling means taking a small portion that represents the whole bulk. A sample must be representative, uncontaminated and large enough for replicate measurements. Solid heaps need random increments; liquids need mixing before sampling. Calibration compares an instrument response with known standards. Run a blank, use at least three standards across the expected range, plot response against concentration, and check the line. The calibration curve is valid only within its linear range.

sections.heading: Volumetric and gravimetric
sections.text: Volumetric analysis measures the volume of a solution of known concentration that reacts with the analyte. Gravimetric analysis measures the mass of a pure precipitate or residue. In gravimetry, filter, wash, dry or ignite to constant mass, then calculate from the formula. Both methods need clean glassware; volumetric analysis also needs careful reading of the meniscus. Example: 25.0 cm³ of hydrochloric acid needs 24.40 cm³ of 0.100 mol/dm³ sodium hydroxide. Moles NaOH = 0.100 × 24.40 ÷ 1000 = 0.002440 mol. The acid reacts 1:1, so acid concentration = 0.002440 ÷ 0.0250 = 0.0976 mol/dm³.

sections.heading: Titrations
sections.text: An acid-base titration finds the equivalence point, where acid and base have reacted in the mole ratio of the equation. A suitable indicator changes colour near that pH. A redox titration uses a reaction in which electrons are transferred. Potassium permanganate is its own indicator in acidic solution: it is purple when oxidised and colourless when reduced. Standardise the titrant first, and repeat titrations until concordant results agree closely.

sections.heading: Spectroscopy
sections.text: UV-visible spectroscopy measures absorption of light by electrons excited between molecular orbitals. The Beer-Lambert law is A = εbc, where A is absorbance, ε is molar absorptivity, b is path length and c is concentration. Infrared spectroscopy measures absorption by molecular vibrations; different bonds absorb at characteristic wavenumbers. Atomic absorption spectroscopy atomises the sample and measures light absorbed by ground-state atoms at a wavelength specific to one element. It is good for trace metals.

keyPoints: A representative sample is uncontaminated and large enough for replicate measurements.
Calibrate with a blank and known standards, and use the curve only within its linear range.
Volumetric analysis uses a measured volume; gravimetric analysis uses a measured mass.
At equivalence, moles react in the ratio of the balanced equation; repeat until concordant.
For titration, moles = concentration × volume in dm³.
Beer-Lambert law: A = εbc; IR shows bond vibrations; AAS measures element-specific atomic absorption.

en.title: Laboratory safety and chemical hygiene
en.short: Hazard labels, SDS, risk assessment, PPE, fume hoods, waste, emergencies and records.

sections.heading: Labels and risk
sections.text:
Chemical containers carry hazard labels. Under the Globally Harmonised System (GHS), labels show pictograms, a signal word, hazard statements and precautionary statements. The safety data sheet (SDS) gives fuller information: hazards, handling, first aid, spill response and disposal.

A risk assessment asks what could harm whom. Identify the hazard, decide who may be exposed, and set controls. Follow the hierarchy of control: eliminate or substitute the chemical, use engineering controls such as a fume hood, then administrative controls, and use personal protective equipment (PPE) last. Record and review the assessment.

sections.heading: PPE and hoods
sections.text:
PPE usually means a fastened lab coat, splash goggles, suitable gloves and closed shoes. Choose gloves tested against the chemical; a glove that resists one solvent may let another through. Remove gloves before touching handles, phones or your face.

A fume hood draws vapours away from the worker. Use it for volatile toxic, corrosive or smelly substances. Keep the sash low, do not block air slots, and check the airflow indicator. A hood is not storage.

sections.heading: Waste and emergencies
sections.text:
Segregate waste at source. Keep halogenated and non-halogenated organic solvents apart, and keep acids, bases, heavy-metal solutions, sharps and broken glass in labelled containers. Never mix waste streams unless allowed. Ask before pouring anything down a sink.

Know exits, eyewash, safety shower, spill kit and fire extinguisher before starting. If a spill occurs, warn others, leave the area and tell the supervisor; clean only if trained and equipped. For eye contact, use eyewash and get help.

Case: Ada finds a cracked acetone bottle in a Lagos laboratory. She warns others, closes the area and tells the technician; she does not wipe it without a spill kit.

sections.heading: Records
sections.text: Record work as you do it, in ink, in a bound notebook or electronic system. Write date, reagents, amounts, conditions, observations, deviations and results. Never erase errors: draw one line through them and initial the change. Good records allow repetition and support investigations.

keyPoints: Read the hazard label and the safety data sheet before using a chemical.
Risk assessment identifies hazards, exposure and controls; PPE is the last line of defence.
Use a fume hood for volatile toxic or corrosive substances and keep the sash low.
Segregate waste streams at source and never mix them unless local rules allow.
Know emergency equipment and report spills; clean up only if trained and equipped.
Record work in ink as it happens, including amounts, observations and deviations.

en.title: Material and energy balances for chemical processes
en.short: System boundaries, steady-state mass and energy balances, recycle, bypass, purge and flowsheet calculations.

sections.heading: Boundaries and mass balances
sections.text: A system boundary is the line around the equipment or process you study. Everything outside is the surroundings. A steady-state balance assumes no accumulation with time. For total mass: input = output. For each species without reaction, the same holds. With reaction: input + generation = output + consumption, using stoichiometry. Choose a basis, such as 100 kg or 1 kmol feed, and keep units consistent.

sections.heading: Recycle, bypass and purge
sections.text: A recycle stream returns part of an outlet to an earlier point; it raises the overall conversion of fresh feed. Recycle ratio is recycle flow divided by fresh feed flow, but state the convention. A bypass splits feed around a unit to control composition or temperature. A purge is a small bleed that removes inert material; without it, inerts build up in a recycle loop. In a flowsheet, solve units in order or balance around the whole loop.

sections.heading: Energy balances
sections.text: An energy balance accounts for enthalpy carried by streams and heat added or removed. At steady state: Σ input enthalpies + Q = Σ output enthalpies, ignoring kinetic and potential energy changes and shaft work; Q is heat added to the system. Sensible enthalpy change is ΔH = m cp ΔT, where cp is specific heat capacity. Reaction contributes ΔH reaction per mole reacted; exothermic reactions release heat. Use consistent reference states.

sections.heading: Worked flowsheet example
sections.text: Fresh feed is 100 kg/h of A. The reactor converts 50% of A per pass to P. The separator recycles all unreacted A and sends P out. Let R be recycled A. Around the reactor: A in = 100 + R; A out = 0.5(100 + R). The separator returns all A out, so R = 0.5(100 + R). Thus R = 100 kg/h and A out = 100 kg/h. P formed = 100 kg/h. Check: feed + recycle = 200 kg/h; product + recycle = 200 kg/h. Cooling the reactor effluent (200 kg/h) from 80°C to 30°C with cp = 4 kJ/(kg·K): heat removed = 200 × 4 × 50 = 40,000 kJ/h, about 11.1 kW.

keyPoints: At steady state, total mass balance is input = output; with reaction, input + generation = output + consumption.
Choose a basis and keep all units consistent before solving a flowsheet.
Recycle returns unreacted material; purge prevents inert build-up; bypass splits feed around a unit.
Energy balance at steady state: Σ input enthalpies + Q = Σ output enthalpies, neglecting shaft work and kinetic and potential changes.
Sensible enthalpy change is ΔH = m cp ΔT; reaction enthalpy is per mole reacted.
In a recycle loop, solve the balance around the reactor and separator together.

en.title: Unit operations: mass and heat transfer
en.short: Equilibrium stages, distillation, absorption, extraction, adsorption, drying, crystallisation, filtration, heat transfer

sections.heading: Equilibrium stages
sections.text: A unit operation separates or changes a mixture by physical means. An equilibrium stage is an ideal contactor in which the leaving streams reach equilibrium. Real stages are less effective, so we use a stage efficiency. For distillation, absorption and extraction, size is often counted in theoretical stages; for packed columns it is counted in transfer units. The operating line is the mass balance around a stage, and the equilibrium curve gives the leaving compositions. The distance between them shows the driving force.

sections.heading: Mass transfer operations
sections.text:
Distillation separates liquids by boiling point; vapour rises and reflux returns liquid. Absorption dissolves a gas solute into a liquid. Extraction moves a solute from one liquid into a second solvent. Leaching extracts a solute from a solid with a solvent. Adsorption holds molecules on a solid surface, as in activated carbon. Drying removes water or solvent by evaporation. Crystallisation forms solid crystals from a solution or melt. Filtration separates solids from a liquid by a filter medium.

Example: one equilibrium extraction stage. 100 kg of solution contains 10 kg solute and 90 kg water. Add 100 kg fresh solvent; distribution coefficient K = 2 (kg solute per kg solvent divided by kg solute per kg water). Let x be solute per kg water and y per kg solvent. Then y = 2x and 90x + 100y = 10. So 290x = 10, x = 0.0345, y = 0.0690. The solvent holds 6.90 kg, so 69.0% is extracted.

sections.heading: Heat transfer operations
sections.text: A heat exchanger transfers heat between two fluids without mixing them. Its duty is Q = U A ΔTlm, where U is the overall heat transfer coefficient, A the area and ΔTlm the log mean temperature difference. Evaporation removes solvent by boiling a solution; multiple-effect evaporators reuse vapour from one effect to heat the next, so less steam is needed. Crystallisation and drying also need heat, so heat and mass transfer are often coupled.

keyPoints: An equilibrium stage is an ideal contactor whose leaving streams are in equilibrium; real stages use an efficiency.
Distillation separates by boiling point; absorption, extraction and leaching transfer a solute between phases.
Adsorption holds solute on a solid surface; drying removes volatile liquid; crystallisation forms solid crystals; filtration separates solids by a filter medium.
For one equilibrium extraction stage, solute balance plus the distribution coefficient gives the split; in the example 69.0% was extracted.
Heat exchanger duty: Q = U A ΔTlm, with ΔTlm the log mean temperature difference.
Evaporation boils off solvent; multiple-effect evaporators reuse vapour to cut steam use.

en.title: Applied chemical thermodynamics for industrial processes
en.short: Applied Gibbs energy, fugacity and activity, phase and reaction equilibria, and industrial equilibrium limits.

sections.heading: Gibbs energy and fugacity
sections.text: Chemical potential μ is the partial molar Gibbs energy. For a real gas, μ = μ° + RT ln(f ÷ f°), where fugacity f is an effective pressure replacing ideal partial pressure. The fugacity coefficient φ = f ÷ P measures nonideality. For a component in a liquid or solid mixture, μ = μ° + RT ln a, where activity a is its effective concentration relative to a standard state. Activity coefficient γ relates a to mole fraction x by a = γx. In ideal cases φ and γ approach 1.

sections.heading: Phase equilibrium
sections.text: Phases α and β are in equilibrium when μiα = μiβ for every component i, or equivalently fiα = fiβ. This gives vapour-liquid equilibrium, yiφiP = xiγiP_sat, where P_sat is saturated vapour pressure. It also explains solvent extraction and crystallisation: a solute distributes until its activity, not concentration, is equal in each phase. Activity coefficients must be measured or estimated.

sections.heading: Reaction equilibrium
sections.text: For a reaction, ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q, where Q is the reaction quotient. At equilibrium ΔG = 0, so K = exp(−ΔG° ÷ RT) and Q = K. K depends on temperature: the van’t Hoff equation, d ln K ÷ dT = ΔH° ÷ (RT²), shows that an exothermic reaction has a smaller K as T rises. Pressure does not change K at fixed temperature; it changes Q and, for real gases, the fugacity coefficients, so the equilibrium composition shifts. Example: A ⇌ B with ΔG° = +5.0 kJ/mol at 400 K. K = exp(−5000 ÷ (8.314 × 400)) = exp(−1.503) = 0.222. Starting with 1 mol A, K = x ÷ (1 − x), so x = 0.182 mol.

sections.heading: Industrial examples
sections.text: Industrial equilibrium-limited processes include ammonia synthesis, N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3, where high pressure favours ammonia but moderate temperature keeps the rate practical; steam reforming and water-gas shift; sulphur dioxide oxidation; methanol synthesis; and esterification. Recycle returns unreacted feed, so overall yield can be high even when each pass is incomplete.

keyPoints: Chemical potential is μ = μ° + RT ln a, with activity a = γx for condensed phases and fugacity f replacing pressure for gases.
Phase equilibrium requires equal chemical potential, or equal fugacity, for each component in every phase.
Reaction equilibrium satisfies ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q = 0, so K = exp(−ΔG° ÷ RT).
The van’t Hoff equation d ln K ÷ dT = ΔH° ÷ (RT²) gives the temperature effect on K.
Pressure does not change K at fixed temperature; it changes Q and the equilibrium composition.
Industrial processes such as ammonia synthesis and steam reforming are equilibrium-limited, so recycle and operating conditions are used to raise overall conversion.

en.title: Reaction kinetics and reactor design
en.short: Rate laws from data, batch, CSTR and PFR design, conversion, selectivity and sizing.

sections.heading: Rate laws from data
sections.text: The rate of A → products is −r_A = −dC_A/dt in a constant-volume batch. A rate law −r_A = k C_A^n gives rate constant k and order n. For initial rates, double C_A0 and compare rates. If C_A0 rises from 0.10 to 0.20 mol/L and the initial rate rises from 2.0 × 10⁻³ to 8.0 × 10⁻³ mol/(L·s), the ratio is 4 = 2^n, so n = 2. Then k = 2.0 × 10⁻³ ÷ 0.10² = 0.20 L/(mol·s). Integrated tests confirm orders.

sections.heading: Batch and flow reactors
sections.text:
A batch reactor has no flow, so composition changes with time. At constant volume, t = N_A0 ∫ dX ÷ (−r_A V); for first order, t = (1/k) ln[1 ÷ (1 − X)].

A continuous stirred-tank reactor (CSTR) is perfectly mixed, so outlet and contents have the same composition: V = F_A0 X ÷ (−r_A). A plug-flow reactor (PFR) has no axial mixing: V = F_A0 ∫ dX ÷ (−r_A). Residence time τ = V ÷ v0.

sections.heading: Conversion and selectivity
sections.text: Conversion is the fraction of A reacted: X = (F_A0 − F_A) ÷ F_A0 for flow, or (N_A0 − N_A) ÷ N_A0 for batch. Selectivity compares desired with undesired product; definitions vary, so state yours. Instantaneous selectivity is desired formation rate divided by undesired formation rate; overall selectivity uses moles. Yield is moles of desired product divided by moles of A fed or by the theoretical maximum. In parallel reactions, selectivity often depends on concentration, so reactor choice matters.

sections.heading: Sizing example
sections.text:
Sizing example: A → products, first order, k = 0.1 min⁻¹, v0 = 100 L/min, C_A0 = 0.10 mol/L, X = 0.90; constant density, isothermal.
CSTR: V = v0 X ÷ [k(1 − X)] = 100 × 0.90 ÷ (0.1 × 0.10) = 9000 L.
PFR: V = (v0 ÷ k) ln[1 ÷ (1 − X)] = (100 ÷ 0.1) ln 10 = 2303 L.
The PFR is about one quarter the size; the CSTR stays at low outlet concentration.

keyPoints: Rate law: −r_A = k C_A^n; find n from a log-log plot of initial rate against C_A0.
Batch design: t = N_A0 ∫ dX ÷ (−r_A V); for first-order constant volume, t = (1/k) ln[1 ÷ (1 − X)].
CSTR design: V = F_A0 X ÷ (−r_A), with −r_A at outlet conditions; for first order, V = v0 X ÷ [k(1 − X)].
PFR design: V = F_A0 ∫ dX ÷ (−r_A); for first-order constant density, V = (v0 ÷ k) ln[1 ÷ (1 − X)].
Residence time τ = V ÷ v0; conversion X = (F_A0 − F_A) ÷ F_A0 for flow.
Selectivity compares desired with undesired product; state the definition used, and remember yield is based on reactant fed or theoretical maximum.

en.title: Industrial catalysis
en.short: Homogeneous and heterogeneous catalysts, supports, promoters, poisoning, regeneration and selection.

sections.heading: Homogeneous and heterogeneous
sections.text: A catalyst speeds a reaction without being consumed overall. A homogeneous catalyst is in the same phase as the reactants, usually a liquid or gas. It has uniform active sites and is easy to study, but separating it from products can be hard. A heterogeneous catalyst is in a different phase, normally a solid with gas or liquid reactants. Reaction occurs on its surface, so high surface area matters. Supports such as silica or alumina disperse the active phase, give strength and help heat transfer. Example: soluble acid catalysts are homogeneous; iron in ammonia synthesis is heterogeneous.

sections.heading: Promoters and deactivation
sections.text: A promoter is added in small amount to improve activity, selectivity or stability without being the main active component. In ammonia synthesis, potassium oxide is a promoter on iron; alumina helps keep the iron surface stable. A poison binds strongly to active sites or reacts with them, lowering activity. Sulphur compounds poison many metal catalysts. Coke, a carbon deposit, blocks cracking catalysts. Regeneration restores activity, often by burning coke in air or by steaming. If poisoning is permanent, the catalyst must be replaced.

sections.heading: Selecting a catalyst
sections.text: Selection balances activity, selectivity, stability, cost and ease of separation. The catalyst must also suit the temperature and pressure. Ammonia synthesis uses promoted iron because it is cheap and robust at high pressure. The contact process for sulphuric acid uses vanadium(V) oxide on a silica support, with potassium sulphate as promoter; it is cheaper and less easily poisoned than platinum. Catalytic cracking uses acidic zeolites, whose pores shape selectivity and whose coke is burned off in a regenerator. A simple selectivity check: if 100 mol of reactant gives 90 mol desired product and 10 mol by-product, selectivity is 90 ÷ (90 + 10) = 0.90, or 90%.

keyPoints: A catalyst speeds a reaction without being consumed overall.
Homogeneous catalysts share the reactant phase; heterogeneous catalysts are usually solids and act at the surface.
Supports disperse the active phase, and promoters improve performance without being the main active component.
Poisoning blocks active sites; regeneration by burning coke or steaming can restore activity.
Catalyst choice balances activity, selectivity, stability, cost and ease of separation.
Ammonia synthesis uses promoted iron, sulphuric acid uses vanadium(V) oxide on silica, and catalytic cracking uses acidic zeolites.

en.title: Process control and instrumentation
en.short: Sensors, feedback loops, PID control, block diagrams, alarms and safety interlocks.

sections.heading: Sensors and signals
sections.text: A sensor measures a process variable; a transmitter converts the measurement into a standard signal, commonly 4-20 mA or a digital fieldbus signal. Temperature sensors include the thermocouple, which produces a small voltage, and the resistance temperature detector (RTD), whose resistance rises with temperature. Pressure is measured by Bourdon tubes, diaphragms or strain gauges. Flow is often inferred from the pressure drop across an orifice plate, or measured directly by Coriolis or ultrasonic meters. Level uses floats, differential pressure, ultrasonic or radar. Composition analysers include gas chromatographs, infrared analysers, pH electrodes and oxygen analysers.

sections.heading: Feedback loop and PID
sections.text:
A feedback loop compares the measured variable with the setpoint. The error e = setpoint − measurement drives a controller. In a block diagram, the setpoint enters a summing junction, the error goes to the controller, the controller output goes to a final control element, the valve affects the process, and the sensor/transmitter returns the measurement to the summing junction.

PID control combines three terms: output = Kp e + Ki ∫e dt + Kd de/dt, plus a bias. Proportional action responds to present error; integral action removes steady offset; derivative action responds to rate of change and can be noisy. Tuning sets Kp, Ki and Kd.

Example: a temperature transmitter spans 0-200 °C and the proportional band is 20%, so 20% of span is 40 °C. An error of 5 °C is 5 ÷ 40 = 0.125 of the band. With a 4-20 mA output, that is 0.125 × 16 mA = 2 mA change. The sign depends on direct or reverse action.

sections.heading: Alarms and interlocks
sections.text: Alarms warn the operator when a variable passes a limit. A safety interlock is automatic: it trips a valve, stops a pump or shuts down a heater when a dangerous condition occurs. Interlocks belong to a safety instrumented system (SIS), which should be independent of the basic control loop. Its required reliability is set by a safety integrity level (SIL). Regular proof testing checks that the interlock still works.

keyPoints: A transmitter converts a sensor signal into a standard signal such as 4-20 mA.
A feedback loop drives the error e = setpoint − measurement towards zero.
PID output = Kp e + Ki ∫e dt + Kd de/dt plus a bias.
Proportional band links error to output change; a 20% band over a 200 °C span is 40 °C.
Alarms warn the operator; interlocks trip equipment automatically and should be independent of basic control.
Check sensor range, controller action and interlock proof tests before trusting a loop.

en.title: Process economics and project evaluation
en.short: Capital and operating costs, depreciation, cash flow, payback, NPV and sensitivity analysis.

sections.heading: Cost estimates
sections.text: Capital cost is the money to build and start the plant: equipment, installation, buildings and working capital. The fixed part splits into inside battery limits (ISBL, process units) and outside battery limits (OSBL, storage, utilities, offices). A contingency covers uncertainty. Operating cost is the yearly cost of running: raw materials, energy, labour, maintenance and overheads. Estimates improve from order-of-magnitude to definitive as design grows. Cost indices update figures to a new date. Prices and rates vary by country and year; use current local data.

sections.heading: Depreciation and cash flow
sections.text: Depreciation spreads capital cost over asset life in the accounts; it is not cash. Straight-line: D = (C − S) ÷ n, where C is installed cost, S salvage value, n life in years. Tax rules set method and life; they differ by country. Cash flow after tax = (revenue − operating cost − depreciation) × (1 − tax rate) + depreciation. Depreciation is added back because it reduced taxable profit without leaving the bank account.

sections.heading: Payback and NPV
sections.text:
Payback is the time for cumulative cash flow to equal the initial investment. It ignores time value and later cash flows. Net present value (NPV) discounts every cash flow to today: NPV = Σ CFt ÷ (1 + r)^t − I0. Accept if NPV is positive.

Example: I0 = 100, CF = 30 each year for 5 years, r = 10%. Payback = 100 ÷ 30 = 3.33 years. Annuity factor = (1 − 1.1^−5) ÷ 0.1 = 3.7908. NPV = 30 × 3.7908 − 100 = 13.72. Positive, so accept.

sections.heading: Sensitivity analysis
sections.text: Sensitivity analysis changes one input at a time and recalculates NPV. Test raw material price, product price, capital cost, exchange rate and plant utilisation. If annual cash flow falls to 25, NPV = 25 × 3.7908 − 100 = −5.23, so the project becomes unacceptable. Scenario analysis changes several inputs together. Break-even analysis finds the output level at which revenue equals total cost, so profit is zero. They show which assumptions matter most but do not remove risk.

keyPoints: Capital cost covers building and starting the plant; operating cost covers running it each year.
Straight-line depreciation: D = (C − S) ÷ n; it is an accounting charge, not cash.
Cash flow after tax = (revenue − operating cost − depreciation) × (1 − tax rate) + depreciation.
Payback = initial investment ÷ annual cash flow when cash flow is constant; it ignores time value.
NPV = Σ CFt ÷ (1 + r)^t − I0; accept a project when NPV is positive.
Sensitivity analysis changes one input at a time to show which assumptions most affect NPV.

en.title: Plant safety and risk management
en.short: Hazard identification, HAZOP, fire and explosion, toxic release, relief systems, safer design and emergency planning.

sections.heading: Hazard identification
sections.text: Process safety starts by finding what can go wrong before it does. Hazard identification uses checklists, what-if analysis, failure modes and effects analysis (FMEA) and hazard and operability studies (HAZOP). A hazard is a source of harm; risk combines how likely harm is with how severe it would be. A risk matrix ranks scenarios so effort goes to the highest risks. It is a ranking tool, not a precise frequency.

sections.heading: HAZOP
sections.text: HAZOP is a structured team review of a process drawing, usually a piping and instrument diagram. The team divides the plant into nodes and applies guide words such as no, more, less, reverse and as well as to each parameter, for example flow. For each deviation it records causes, consequences and safeguards, then actions. Case: on a tank-filling node, guide word more with flow means a higher flow than design. Causes include a failed inlet valve; consequences include overfilling, vapour release and fire; safeguards include a high-level alarm and independent trip. The action may be to add a redundant level trip.

sections.heading: Fire, explosion, toxic release
sections.text: Fire needs fuel, oxygen and an ignition source. Flammable liquids release vapour; a vapour cloud can explode if confined or congested. Dust explosions occur with fine combustible powders. Toxic release is assessed by source rate, dispersion and exposure limits. Prevention includes control of ignition, ventilation, detection and emergency shutdown.

sections.heading: Relief, design, planning
sections.text: Relief systems protect equipment from overpressure. Pressure relief valves and rupture discs discharge to a safe location such as a flare or scrubber; they must not be blocked. Inherently safer design follows minimise, substitute, moderate and simplify. Emergency planning covers alarms, evacuation, muster points, drills, communication and mutual aid. Local safety regulations vary by country. In Nigeria the Factories Act and its regulations apply; the UK uses the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974 and COMAH 2015; the US uses OSHA’s Process Safety Management standard and EPA’s Risk Management Program. Check the current official text.

keyPoints: Hazard identification methods include checklists, what-if analysis, FMEA and HAZOP.
HAZOP uses guide words at nodes to find deviations, causes, consequences and safeguards.
Fire needs fuel, oxygen and ignition; vapour and dust clouds can explode.
Relief valves and rupture discs protect equipment from overpressure and must discharge safely.
Inherently safer design order is minimise, substitute, moderate and simplify.
Emergency plans need alarms, evacuation, drills and communication; regulations vary by country.

en.title: Environmental management and green chemistry
en.short: Waste minimisation, cleaner production, atom economy, effluent treatment and impact assessment.

sections.heading: Waste minimisation
sections.text:
Waste minimisation means avoiding waste at source rather than treating it after it forms. The waste hierarchy runs prevent, reduce, reuse, recycle, recover, treat, dispose. Cleaner production applies this preventive idea continuously to processes, products and services, looking for wasted raw material, energy and water.

Example: recovering and reusing cleaning solvent cuts purchase cost and solvent vapour emissions. Source reduction often costs less than end-of-pipe treatment, but it needs good process data and operator involvement.

sections.heading: Atom economy
sections.text:
Atom economy measures the share of reactant mass that becomes the desired product: atom economy = (mass of desired product ÷ total mass of reactants) × 100. It is not yield, which is product actually obtained.

Example: reactants of 100 g/mol and 50 g/mol give 120 g/mol of desired product and 30 g/mol of by-product.
Atom economy = 120 ÷ 150 × 100 = 80%

Green chemistry designs chemical products and processes to reduce or eliminate the use and generation of hazardous substances. It also counts solvent, energy and catalyst, so high atom economy alone does not make a process green.

sections.heading: Effluent and emissions
sections.text:
Effluent is liquid waste; emissions are releases to air. Treatment matches the pollutant. Settling, filtration and flotation remove solids. Neutralisation, precipitation and oxidation change dissolved chemicals. Activated sludge uses micro-organisms to break down biodegradable organic matter.

Air streams may pass through cyclones, bag filters, electrostatic precipitators, scrubbers or adsorption beds. Treated streams are monitored against permit limits, and sludge or spent adsorbent must be managed. Limits differ by country, so check the current national regulator.

sections.heading: Impact assessment
sections.text:
Environmental impact assessment (EIA) predicts likely effects of a proposed project before approval. It usually covers baseline conditions, alternatives, significant impacts, mitigation and monitoring, with public consultation. The output is a report and, in many countries, approval with conditions.

Legal requirements vary, so check the current national environmental regulator and the project location. Environmental management systems such as ISO 14001 help a site manage these duties continuously.

keyPoints: Waste minimisation follows a hierarchy: prevent, reduce, reuse, recycle, recover, treat, dispose.
Cleaner production prevents waste at source rather than treating it at the end of the pipe.
Atom economy = (mass of desired product ÷ total mass of reactants) × 100.
Atom economy is not the same as percentage yield.
Effluent and emission treatment must suit the pollutant and meet permit limits.
Environmental impact assessment predicts effects before approval; rules vary by country, so check the national regulator.

en.title: Heavy inorganic chemicals and fertilisers
en.short: Sulphuric acid, ammonia, nitric acid, chlor-alkali, soda ash and N, P, K fertiliser manufacture.

sections.heading: Sulphuric acid
sections.text:
The contact process makes sulphuric acid. Sulphur burns to SO2, then is oxidised over a vanadium(V) oxide catalyst: 2SO2 + O2 ⇌ 2SO3. The reaction is exothermic, so about 400-450°C balances yield against rate. SO3 is absorbed in concentrated sulphuric acid to give oleum, which is then diluted; adding SO3 to water directly makes a corrosive mist.

Example: burning 32 g of sulphur (1 mol) gives 1 mol SO2, which needs 0.5 mol O2 and can give 1 mol SO3, then 1 mol H2SO4, that is 98 g.

sections.heading: Ammonia and nitric acid
sections.text:
Haber-Bosch ammonia: N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3 over iron. High pressure and low temperature favour ammonia, but the catalyst needs about 400-500°C, so plants compromise and recycle unreacted gas. Conditions differ by plant.

Ostwald nitric acid: ammonia is oxidised over platinum-rhodium gauze to NO (4NH3 + 5O2 → 4NO + 6H2O), NO becomes NO2, and NO2 absorbs in water: 3NO2 + H2O → 2HNO3 + NO. The NO is recycled.

sections.heading: Chlor-alkali and soda ash
sections.text:
Chlor-alkali: electrolysis of brine gives chlorine at the anode and hydrogen and sodium hydroxide at the cathode: 2NaCl + 2H2O → 2NaOH + Cl2 + H2. Membrane cells are now usual.

Soda ash (Solvay): brine saturated with ammonia and carbon dioxide precipitates sodium hydrogencarbonate: NaCl + NH3 + CO2 + H2O → NaHCO3 + NH4Cl. Heating gives Na2CO3. Ammonia is recovered.

sections.heading: Fertilisers and NPK
sections.text:
Nitrogen fertilisers include ammonium nitrate, urea and ammonium sulphate; phosphorus comes from rock phosphate treated with acid to give superphosphate or phosphoric acid; potassium comes as mined potash (potassium chloride). NPK blending mixes these to a grade such as 20-10-10, meaning 20% N, 10% P2O5 and 10% K2O by mass.

Example: 100 kg of 20-10-10 contains 20 kg N, 10 kg P2O5 and 10 kg K2O.

keyPoints: Contact process: 2SO2 + O2 ⇌ 2SO3 over V2O5 at about 400-450°C, with SO3 absorbed in concentrated acid.
Haber-Bosch: N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3 over iron at high pressure, with unreacted gas recycled.
Ostwald: 4NH3 + 5O2 → 4NO + 6H2O, then 3NO2 + H2O → 2HNO3 + NO.
Chlor-alkali: 2NaCl + 2H2O → 2NaOH + Cl2 + H2.
Solvay: NaCl + NH3 + CO2 + H2O → NaHCO3 + NH4Cl, and heating NaHCO3 gives Na2CO3.
An NPK grade such as 20-10-10 means 20% N, 10% P2O5 and 10% K2O by mass.

en.title: Petroleum refining and petrochemicals
en.short: Crude oil distillation, cracking, reforming, alkylation and main petrochemical products.

sections.heading: Crude oil distillation
sections.text: Crude oil is a mixture of hydrocarbons with a range of boiling points. Fractional distillation separates it into fractions by boiling range. Atmospheric distillation gives refinery gas, liquefied petroleum gas, naphtha, kerosene, gas oil and atmospheric residue. The residue is distilled under vacuum because lower pressure lowers boiling point and avoids thermal cracking. Each fraction is still a mixture, and cut points (the boiling-range boundaries) vary with the crude and the refinery. Approximate ranges are naphtha about 30 to 180 °C, kerosene about 150 to 250 °C and gas oil about 250 to 350 °C.

sections.heading: Cracking and reforming
sections.text: Cracking breaks large hydrocarbon molecules into smaller alkenes and alkanes. Steam cracking is thermal cracking of light feeds such as ethane or naphtha at high temperature; naphtha cracking gives ethylene, propylene, butadiene and aromatics, while ethane cracking gives mainly ethylene. Catalytic cracking uses a zeolite catalyst to make gasoline components, and hydrocracking adds hydrogen. Reforming rearranges straight-chain alkanes and naphthenes (cycloalkanes) into branched alkanes and aromatics. This raises the octane number, a measure of a fuel’s resistance to engine knock. Catalytic reforming uses a platinum-containing catalyst and produces reformate, the high-octane liquid product, plus hydrogen.

sections.heading: Alkylation and feedstocks
sections.text: Alkylation joins isobutane with a light olefin such as propylene or isobutylene to make branched, high-octane gasoline components. It uses an acid catalyst such as sulphuric acid, hydrofluoric acid or a solid acid. The main petrochemical feedstocks are ethylene, propylene, butadiene, benzene, toluene, xylenes, methane and synthesis gas, a mixture of carbon monoxide and hydrogen. Ethylene gives polyethylene, ethylene oxide, ethylene glycol and, through ethylene dichloride, PVC. Propylene gives polypropylene, acrylonitrile, propylene oxide and cumene. p-Xylene gives terephthalic acid for PET, and benzene gives styrene, phenol and cyclohexane. Methane gives synthesis gas for methanol and ammonia.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Suppose a steam cracker gives 300 kg of ethylene from 1,000 kg of naphtha, a yield of 0.30. A polyethylene plant needs 250 kg of polymer and its polymerisation yield is 95%. Ethylene needed = 250 ÷ 0.95 = 263.2 kg. Naphtha needed = 263.2 ÷ 0.30 = 877 kg. Losses and other products are ignored, so real figures differ.

keyPoints: Crude oil is separated by fractional distillation into boiling-range fractions, and the residue is vacuum distilled.
Cracking breaks large hydrocarbons into smaller alkenes and alkanes; steam cracking is the main source of ethylene and propylene.
Catalytic reforming rearranges hydrocarbons into branched alkanes and aromatics to raise the octane number.
Alkylation joins isobutane with light olefins to make high-octane branched gasoline components.
Main petrochemical feedstocks include ethylene, propylene, butadiene, benzene, toluene, xylenes, methane and synthesis gas.
Yield calculation: product mass = feed mass × yield, so feed needed = product needed ÷ yield.

en.title: Polymers and polymerisation
en.short: Addition and condensation polymerisation, mechanisms, molecular weight, crystallinity, processing and recycling.

sections.heading: Addition and condensation
sections.text: Addition polymerisation joins unsaturated monomers, such as ethene, without losing a small molecule; the repeat unit has the same atoms as the monomer. It is chain-growth: monomers add to active chain ends. Condensation polymerisation, a step-growth route, joins monomers with two functional groups and usually releases water or HCl. Polyethylene terephthalate from ethylene glycol and terephthalic acid, and nylon from a diamine and a diacid, are examples. High conversion gives high molecular weight.

sections.heading: Mechanisms
sections.text: Free-radical polymerisation uses an initiator that forms radicals. Initiation adds a radical to a monomer; propagation grows the chain; termination combines or disproportionates radicals. Chain transfer limits chain length. It makes polyethylene, polystyrene, polyvinyl chloride and poly(methyl methacrylate). Ionic polymerisation uses anionic or cationic active centres; living anionic polymerisation gives narrow molecular-weight distributions. Coordination polymerisation uses a transition-metal catalyst, such as Ziegler-Natta, to insert monomer into a metal-carbon bond; it gives linear chains and controls stereochemistry, producing high-density polyethylene and isotactic polypropylene.

sections.heading: Molecular weight and crystallinity
sections.text: Molecular weight is averaged because chains vary. Number-average Mn = ΣNiMi ÷ ΣNi; weight-average Mw = ΣNiMi² ÷ ΣNiMi; dispersity Đ = Mw ÷ Mn. Example: equal moles of 10,000 and 90,000 g/mol give Mn = (10,000 + 90,000) ÷ 2 = 50,000 g/mol and Mw = (10,000² + 90,000²) ÷ (10,000 + 90,000) = 82,000 g/mol, so Đ = 1.64. Crystallinity needs regular chains that pack. Stereoregularity, slow cooling and annealing raise it; irregular groups, branching and crosslinks lower it. Semicrystalline plastics have crystalline lamellae in an amorphous matrix, with a glass transition Tg and melting point Tm.

sections.heading: Processing and recycling
sections.text: Processing melts or softens polymer: extrusion for pipes and film, injection moulding for parts, blow moulding for bottles. Rubber is crosslinked by vulcanisation, usually with sulphur. Thermoplastics can be sorted, reground and remelted, though repeated heating degrades them. Thermosets and vulcanised rubber cannot be remelted; they may be ground, depolymerised or burned for energy. Chemical recycling recovers monomers or oils, but economics vary.

keyPoints: Addition polymerisation is chain-growth and loses no small molecule; condensation polymerisation is step-growth and usually loses one.
Free-radical polymerisation proceeds by initiation, propagation, termination and chain transfer, while ionic and coordination polymerisation use charged or metal-centred active sites.
Number-average molecular weight is Mn = ΣNiMi ÷ ΣNi, weight-average is Mw = ΣNiMi² ÷ ΣNiMi, and dispersity is Đ = Mw ÷ Mn.
Crystallinity is raised by stereoregular chains and slow cooling and lowered by branching, irregular groups and crosslinks.
Thermoplastics can be remelted and recycled mechanically, but thermosets and vulcanised rubber cannot.
Common processing methods are extrusion, injection moulding and blow moulding, and rubber is crosslinked by vulcanisation with sulphur.

en.title: Surfactants, soaps and detergents
en.short: Saponification, soap and synthetic detergents, surfactant types, builders, formulation and environmental effects.

sections.heading: Surfactant structure
sections.text:
A surfactant has a hydrophilic head and a hydrophobic tail. In water it adsorbs at interfaces and lowers surface tension, allowing grease to lift into micelles.

Types are anionic (soap, linear alkylbenzene sulfonate, LAS), cationic (quaternary ammonium), nonionic (alcohol ethoxylates) and amphoteric (betaines). Anionic surfactants clean best in alkaline wash liquor; nonionics tolerate hard water; cationics are used as fabric softeners and biocides.

sections.heading: Saponification
sections.text:
Saponification is the alkaline hydrolysis of a triglyceride to glycerol and soap, the alkali salt of a fatty acid. For triolein:
C57H104O6 + 3 NaOH -> C3H8O3 + 3 C17H33COONa

Using molar masses 885.45, 40.00, 92.09 and 304.45 g/mol, 1.000 kg triolein needs 3 × (1000 ÷ 885.45) × 40.00 = 135.5 g NaOH and gives 3 × (1000 ÷ 885.45) × 304.45 = 1031.5 g sodium oleate plus (1000 ÷ 885.45) × 92.09 = 104.0 g glycerol. Check: 1000 + 135.5 = 1135.5 g in, 1031.5 + 104.0 = 1135.5 g out. Industrial soap may also contain salt, glycerine and small amounts of unsaponified oil.

sections.heading: Soap versus syndets
sections.text:
Soap is biodegradable and cheap but forms insoluble calcium and magnesium salts (scum) in hard water, wasting soap. It also hydrolyses to fatty acid at low pH.

Synthetic detergents (syndets) are often made from petrochemicals. LAS and alcohol ethoxylates tolerate hard water and low pH, and can be blended for liquid or powder products. Their biodegradability depends on structure: linear chains degrade aerobically; highly branched chains persist.

sections.heading: Builders and environment
sections.text:
Builders improve detergent performance by sequestering Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺, supplying alkalinity and buffering pH. Common builders are sodium carbonate, sodium silicate, sodium citrate and zeolites; phosphate builders were effective but caused eutrophication. Formulation balances surfactant, builder, enzymes, bleach, brightener, filler and foam control.

Detergent waste can foam in rivers, harm aquatic life and add nutrients. Wastewater treatment removes much surfactant, but phosphate restrictions and biodegradability testing are needed. Regulations differ by country, so check local rules.

keyPoints: A surfactant has a hydrophilic head and a hydrophobic tail; it lowers surface tension and forms micelles.
Saponification is alkaline hydrolysis of a triglyceride: triglyceride + 3 NaOH -> glycerol + 3 soap.
For triolein, 1.000 kg needs 135.5 g NaOH and gives 1031.5 g sodium oleate plus 104.0 g glycerol.
Soap forms scum with calcium and magnesium in hard water; syndets based on LAS or alcohol ethoxylates tolerate hard water.
Builders such as sodium carbonate, citrate and zeolites soften water and buffer pH; phosphate builders cause eutrophication.
Surfactant biodegradability depends on structure, and detergent regulations differ by country.

en.title: Cement, ceramics and glass
en.short: Portland cement clinker phases and hydration, ceramic forming and firing, and glass structure and batch melting.

sections.heading: Portland cement
sections.text: Portland cement is made by heating limestone and clay at roughly 1450 °C in a kiln. The product, clinker, contains four main phases: alite (C3S), belite (C2S), tricalcium aluminate (C3A) and tetracalcium aluminoferrite (C4AF). Cement notation writes C = CaO, S = SiO2, A = Al2O3 and F = Fe2O3. Alite gives early strength; belite hydrates slowly and gives later strength. C3A reacts fastest and would cause flash set, so gypsum is added to form ettringite and control setting. Hydration produces calcium silicate hydrate (C-S-H), the main binding phase, plus calcium hydroxide. The phase proportions control heat release and strength development.

sections.heading: Ceramic processing
sections.text: Traditional ceramics use clay, silica and feldspar. The body is prepared, formed by pressing, extrusion or slip casting (pouring a stable suspension into a porous mould), dried, then fired. Firing sinters the particles and may vitrify the body, reducing porosity and raising strength. Porosity and firing temperature control strength and durability. The mix design sets the firing schedule. A concrete case: a tile plant must control drying shrinkage before firing, or tiles warp.

sections.heading: Glass structure and manufacture
sections.text: Glass is an amorphous solid: a disordered network, not a crystal. Silica is the network former; Na2O and CaO are modifiers that break bridges and lower viscosity; Al2O3 can enter the network. Soda-lime-silica glass is made by melting a batch of sand, soda ash and limestone, then forming by float, blowing or drawing, and annealing to relieve stress. Annealing is a controlled cooling step. Worked example: to make 1000 kg of glass containing 72% SiO2 from sand that is 90% SiO2, sand needed = 1000 × 0.72 ÷ 0.90 = 800 kg.

keyPoints: Clinker phases are alite (C3S), belite (C2S), C3A and C4AF; cement notation uses C = CaO, S = SiO2, A = Al2O3, F = Fe2O3.
C3S gives early strength, C2S gives later strength, and gypsum controls C3A setting by forming ettringite.
Hydration of Portland cement forms C-S-H, the main binding phase, and calcium hydroxide.
Ceramic processing is form, dry, fire; sintering and vitrification reduce porosity.
Glass is an amorphous network; SiO2 is the former and Na2O or CaO are modifiers.
Raw material mass = required component mass ÷ mass fraction of component in the raw material.

en.title: Corrosion and materials selection
en.short: Electrochemical, galvanic and pitting corrosion, passivation, prevention and plant materials selection.

sections.heading: Electrochemical corrosion
sections.text: Corrosion is the degradation of a metal by chemical or electrochemical reaction with its environment. In electrochemical corrosion, an anodic reaction releases metal ions (Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻) and a cathodic reaction consumes electrons, often oxygen reduction (O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻) or hydrogen evolution. The metal, electrolyte and connection between anodic and cathodic sites form a corrosion cell. The driving force is the potential difference; standard electrode potentials and the galvanic series rank metals. Faraday’s law links current to mass loss.

sections.heading: Galvanic, pitting and passivation
sections.text: Galvanic corrosion occurs when dissimilar metals touch in an electrolyte: the more active metal becomes the anode and corrodes faster. A small anode joined to a large cathode is dangerous because the anode current density is high. Pitting corrosion is local breakdown of a passive film, commonly by chlorides, producing deep pits while most of the surface stays intact. Passivation is the formation of a thin, protective oxide film, as on stainless steel, aluminium and titanium. Chlorides can break the film locally and start pitting; reducing conditions can dissolve the film and cause uniform attack.

sections.heading: Prevention and selection
sections.text:
Prevention includes coatings, cathodic protection (making the metal the cathode with a sacrificial anode or an impressed current), corrosion inhibitors, better design (drainage, avoiding crevices) and material choice. Select materials from corrosion tables for the actual environment: chloride level, pH, temperature, flow and oxidising power. Carbon steel suits dry or mildly corrosive service; stainless steels, alloys, polymers or ceramics suit aggressive conditions. Consider cost, fabrication, strength and codes.

Worked example: a steel pipe (iron, M = 55.85 g/mol, n = 2, ρ = 7,870 kg/m³) has i = 100 µA/cm² = 1 A/m².
r = iM ÷ (nFρ) = 1 × 0.05585 ÷ (2 × 96,485 × 7,870) = 3.68 × 10⁻¹¹ m/s.
r = 3.68 × 10⁻¹¹ × 3.1536 × 10⁷ = 1.16 × 10⁻³ m/year = 1.16 mm/year.

keyPoints: Electrochemical corrosion needs an anode, a cathode, an electrolyte and a metal path.
The more active metal in a galvanic couple becomes the anode and corrodes faster.
Passivation is a thin protective oxide film; chloride breakdown leads to pitting.
Prevention includes coatings, cathodic protection, inhibitors and design that avoids crevices.
Select materials for the real environment, including chloride, pH and temperature.
Faraday’s law: r = iM ÷ (nFρ); 100 µA/cm² on iron gives about 1.16 mm/year.

en.title: Fine chemicals and pharmaceuticals
en.short: This summary covers synthesis, batch and continuous operation, GMP, formulation and quality assurance.

sections.heading: Fine chemicals
sections.text: Fine chemicals are made in small volumes to high purity and high value, often by multi-step organic synthesis. Each step must be selective and reproducible. A pharmaceutical active ingredient (API) is a fine chemical with strict purity limits. Overall yield falls with each step: if three steps give 90%, 85% and 80%, the overall yield is 0.90 × 0.85 × 0.80 = 0.612, or 61.2%. Low overall yield is one reason APIs are expensive.

sections.heading: Batch or continuous
sections.text: Batch operation makes a fixed amount in a vessel, then cleans and changes product. It suits small volumes, many products and complex multi-step routes, and gives clear batch records for traceability. Continuous operation feeds and withdraws material steadily. It gives steadier quality, less material held in the plant at any time and lower cost per unit at large volume, but is less flexible. Continuous manufacturing is accepted by regulators for some medicines, but the choice depends on volume, chemistry and regulation.

sections.heading: GMP and quality
sections.text: Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) is the quality system that ensures a medicine is consistently made to its quality standard. It covers premises, equipment, trained staff, written procedures, cleaning, validation (proving a process does what it claims), documentation and contamination control. GMP is enforced by national regulators; requirements vary, so check the current national code (for example NAFDAC in Nigeria or FDA in the United States).

sections.heading: Formulation and QA
sections.text: Formulation turns an API into a dosage form, such as a tablet, by adding excipients (inactive ingredients) for dose, stability, flow or release. Quality assurance (QA) is the planned system that prevents defects; quality control (QC) is the testing that checks them. QA includes batch records, supplier checks, validation and deviation handling. A batch is released only when QA confirms it meets specification.

keyPoints: Fine chemicals are low-volume, high-value, high-purity products, often made by multi-step synthesis.
The overall yield of a multi-step synthesis is the product of the individual step yields.
Batch operation suits small volumes and many products; continuous operation suits steady, larger-volume production.
Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) is the documented quality system enforced by national medicines regulators.
Formulation combines the active pharmaceutical ingredient with excipients to give a stable, accurate dosage form.
Quality assurance prevents defects through systems and records, while quality control tests materials and products against specification.

en.title: Quality control and industrial analysis
en.short: Sampling, calibration, validation, control charts, specification testing and records.

sections.heading: Sampling
sections.text: Quality control starts with a sample that represents the lot, the batch, tank or shipment being judged. A sampling plan sets how many increments to take, where, and how to combine them. Random sampling avoids bias; a composite sample mixes increments. Sampling error is the difference between sample and lot. Sampling standards vary by product and country, so use the current official method. For a tank, sample top, middle and bottom if the method requires it.

sections.heading: Calibration and validation
sections.text: Calibration compares an instrument with a reference standard of known value and records the result, giving traceability to a stated reference. A calibration curve plots response against concentration. Method validation shows a method is fit for purpose: accuracy, precision, specificity, linearity, range, detection limit, quantification limit and robustness. Example: standards of 0, 1, 2 and 3 mg/L give absorbances 0.00, 0.10, 0.20 and 0.30. The slope is 0.10 per mg/L. A sample absorbance of 0.25 gives 0.25 ÷ 0.10 = 2.5 mg/L.

sections.heading: Statistical quality control
sections.text: Statistical quality control separates normal variation from a real change. A control chart plots a measured value against time with a centre line and control limits, often the mean plus or minus three standard deviations. Points outside the limits, or trends, suggest an assignable cause. Process capability compares the specification width with the process spread. Example: ten purity results have mean 100.0 % and sample standard deviation 0.12 %. Limits for individual values are 100.0 ± 3 × 0.12 = 99.64 to 100.36 %.

sections.heading: Specification and records
sections.text: Specification testing checks identity, purity, strength and physical form against agreed limits. A result near a limit needs its measurement uncertainty considered; often the measured value plus or minus the expanded uncertainty must lie within the specification. Records include batch sheets, raw data, calibration certificates, deviations and certificates of analysis. They must be legible, traceable and kept for the required period. Standards such as ISO 9001, ISO/IEC 17025 and national product standards vary, so confirm the current edition.

keyPoints: A sample must represent the lot; follow the current official sampling plan.
Calibration gives traceability; a linear calibration curve follows y = mx + c, so concentration = (response − c) ÷ m.
Method validation covers accuracy, precision, specificity, linearity, range, detection limit, quantification limit and robustness.
In statistical quality control, control limits are often mean ± 3s; points outside or trends indicate an assignable cause.
Specification testing compares results with limits and should account for measurement uncertainty.
Records must be legible, traceable and kept for the required period; standards vary by country and product, so check the current edition.

en.title: Professional practice, ethics and regulation
en.short: Chemists’ roles, codes, Responsible Care, confidentiality, IP, regulation and safety culture.

sections.heading: Roles and codes
sections.text: Industrial chemists develop products and processes, scale them up, troubleshoot plants, analyse materials and advise on safety, environment and quality. They often work in teams with engineers, technicians and regulators. A professional code is a set of principles a body expects members to follow: competence, honesty, safety, confidentiality and disclosure of conflicts. Codes do not replace the law; they add duties. Registration and protected titles vary by country, so check the national professional body and legislation.

sections.heading: Responsible Care and IP
sections.text: Responsible Care is a voluntary chemical-industry initiative, coordinated internationally by the International Council of Chemical Associations, in which companies commit to manage safety, health and environment beyond legal minimums. Confidentiality means keeping employer and client information private; it is usually backed by contracts and need-to-know rules. Intellectual property (IP) is legally protected knowledge or expression. A patent gives an exclusive right for a limited term in exchange for public disclosure. A trade secret is protected only while it stays secret. Employment contracts often assign inventions to the employer; the rules differ by country.
