sections.heading: Compliance and safety culture
sections.text: Regulatory compliance means meeting the laws and permits that apply to a site: chemical control, transport, emissions, waste, labelling and worker safety. Requirements differ by country and change, so use current official sources. Safety culture is the shared values and behaviour that determine how seriously risks are treated. It shows in management commitment, near-miss reporting, training and a willingness to stop unsafe work. A good code supports speaking up; legal protection for whistleblowers varies.

sections.heading: Case
sections.text: Case: Ada, a process chemist at a fertiliser plant in Nigeria, notices a reactor temperature trend outside its safe operating envelope, the range of conditions the reactor is designed to run in safely. She records the data, tells the shift supervisor and declines to approve the batch until the cause is checked. Her professional duty and the company’s safety culture should support her; retaliation protection depends on Nigerian law and company policy.

keyPoints: Professional codes set duties such as competence, honesty, safety, confidentiality and conflict disclosure.
Responsible Care is a voluntary industry initiative on safety, health and environment beyond legal minimums.
Confidentiality protects employer and client information; patents and trade secrets are different forms of intellectual property.
Regulatory compliance means meeting current national laws and permits; requirements vary by country.
Safety culture is shown by reporting, management commitment and willingness to stop unsafe work.
Registration and legal duties for chemists vary by country, so check the national body and legislation.

en.title: Advanced reaction engineering: non-ideal flow and catalyst limits
en.short: Non-ideal flow, residence time distribution, transfer limits, deactivation and reactor modelling.

sections.heading: Non-ideal flow
sections.text:
Real reactors lie between ideal plug flow and perfect mixing. The residence time distribution (RTD), E(t), is the age distribution of the exit stream: E(t)dt is the fraction of exit fluid with age between t and t+dt. Its mean is τ = ∫ t E(t) dt and variance σ² = ∫ (t−τ)² E(t) dt. For a CSTR, E(t) = (1/τ) exp(−t/τ), so mean τ and variance τ². Tanks in series and axial dispersion models fit measured tracer curves.

Example: a tracer test gives E(t) = (1/10) exp(−t/10) min⁻¹. Mean = 10 min and variance = 100 min², the CSTR result.

sections.heading: Transfer limits
sections.text:
In porous catalysts, reactant crosses an external film and diffuses in pores. External mass transfer rate is kc av (Cb − Cs), where av is external area per reactor volume. Internal diffusion is described by the Thiele modulus. For a first-order reaction in a sphere of radius R, φ = R √(k/D_eff), where D_eff is effective diffusivity. The effectiveness factor η is actual rate ÷ rate without diffusion resistance, and η = (3/φ)(1/tanh φ − 1/φ). Strong diffusion limitation gives η ≈ 3/φ.

Example: φ = 2.0. tanh 2.0 = 0.9640, so η = 1.5 × (1.0373 − 0.5) = 0.806. The pellet delivers about 81% of the intrinsic rate.

Exothermic reactions also face heat transfer limits. Poor heat removal can create hot spots and multiple steady states.

sections.heading: Deactivation and modelling
sections.text: Catalyst deactivation lowers activity a(t) = rate(t) ÷ rate(0). Poisoning blocks sites, fouling deposits block pores, sintering loses surface area, and coking forms carbon. Reactor models combine mole, energy and pressure balances with kinetics, RTD or dispersion, transfer coefficients and a deactivation law. They are checked against tracer tests and pilot-plant data before scale-up.

keyPoints: The RTD E(t) gives the age distribution of exit fluid; mean τ = ∫ t E(t) dt and variance σ² = ∫ (t−τ)² E(t) dt.
For a CSTR, E(t) = (1/τ) exp(−t/τ), so mean = τ and variance = τ².
External mass transfer rate is kc av (Cb − Cs); internal diffusion is measured by the Thiele modulus φ = R √(k/D_eff) for a first-order sphere.
For a sphere, η = (3/φ)(1/tanh φ − 1/φ); strong pore diffusion gives η ≈ 3/φ.
Catalyst activity a(t) = rate(t) ÷ rate(0) falls by poisoning, fouling, sintering or coking.
Reactor models combine mole, energy and pressure balances with kinetics, RTD or dispersion, transfer coefficients and deactivation, then are validated with tracer and pilot data.

en.title: Process modelling and simulation
en.short: Building process models, numerical solvers, flowsheet simulation, validation and sensitivity.

sections.heading: Building models
sections.text: A process model is a set of equations that links inputs, state variables and outputs. Build it from conservation balances, rate laws, equilibrium relations and equipment correlations, then close it with specifications. Lumped models ignore spatial variation and use ordinary differential equations (ODEs); distributed models use partial differential equations. Keep the purpose in view: a model for control needs different detail from one for design.

sections.heading: Numerical solution
sections.text:
Steady-state models give nonlinear algebraic equations, often solved by Newton-Raphson: x(n+1) = x(n) − f(x(n)) ÷ f′(x(n)). Dynamic models give ODEs, solved by Euler, Runge-Kutta or stiff solvers for fast and slow time scales. Euler is y(n+1) = y(n) + Δt f(t(n), y(n)).

Example: dC/dt = −kC, C(0) = 1.0 mol/L, k = 0.1 min−1, Δt = 2 min. Euler gives C1 = 1.0 + 2(−0.1 × 1.0) = 0.80 mol/L. The exact value is e^(−0.2) = 0.8187 mol/L, so the error is 0.0187 mol/L. Smaller steps reduce error but cost more.

sections.heading: Flowsheet simulation
sections.text: A flowsheet is a network of unit-operation models joined by material and energy streams. Sequential modular simulation solves each unit in turn and iterates around recycle streams. Equation-oriented simulation solves all equations together, which suits optimisation but needs good initial values. Simulators provide property packages and unit models; the engineer must still check assumptions.

sections.heading: Validation and sensitivity
sections.text: Validation compares model predictions with independent plant or pilot data. Calibration adjusts uncertain parameters to fit data, but validation must use data not used in calibration. Sensitivity analysis varies inputs or parameters and records the change in outputs. Local sensitivity uses derivatives; global methods sample the range. Use it to find the parameters that matter and to plan experiments. A model is credible only after both steps.

keyPoints: A process model links inputs, states and outputs through balances, rate laws and specifications.
Newton-Raphson solves f(x)=0 by x(n+1)=x(n)−f(x(n))÷f′(x(n)).
Euler solves dy/dt=f(t,y) by y(n+1)=y(n)+Δt f(t(n),y(n)); smaller Δt reduces error.
Flowsheet simulation connects unit models; sequential modular iterates recycles, equation-oriented solves all equations together.
Validation compares predictions with independent data; calibration fits parameters.
Sensitivity analysis ranks parameters by their effect on outputs, using local derivatives or global sampling.

en.title: Advanced materials and nanotechnology
en.short: Nanomaterials, composites, synthesis, characterisation, scale-up and safety.

sections.heading: Materials and scales
sections.text:
Advanced materials are designed to give properties that ordinary bulk materials lack: high strength to weight, tailored conductivity, or controlled release. Nanomaterials have at least one dimension between about 1 and 100 nm. Examples include nanoparticles, carbon nanotubes, graphene and quantum dots (semiconductor nanocrystals). A composite combines a matrix with a reinforcement; the matrix holds the shape and the reinforcement carries load. The rule of mixtures gives an upper bound for aligned continuous fibres: E_c = fE_f + (1 − f)E_m, where f is fibre volume fraction.

Small size raises surface area. For a cube of side L, surface area to volume ratio is 6 ÷ L. A 100 nm cube has 6 ÷ (100 × 10^-9 m) = 6 × 10^7 m^-1. A 1 mm cube has 6 ÷ 10^-3 = 6 × 10^3 m^-1, ten thousand times less. At density 1000 kg/m³ this is 60 m²/g against 0.006 m²/g.

sections.heading: Synthesis and characterisation
sections.text: Synthesis is top-down, such as milling or lithography, or bottom-up, such as sol-gel (a wet chemical route through a sol then a gel), precipitation, chemical vapour deposition and self-assembly. Bottom-up routes can give narrow size distributions but need careful control of concentration, temperature and pH. Characterisation uses electron microscopy for size and shape, X-ray diffraction for crystal structure, dynamic light scattering for particle size in suspension, nitrogen adsorption for surface area, and Raman or X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy for chemistry. No single method is enough.

sections.heading: Scale-up and safety
sections.text: Industrial uses include catalysts, coatings, sensors, batteries, lightweight composites and drug delivery. Scale-up is difficult because mixing, heat removal and residence time change with vessel size; nanoparticles can stick together (agglomerate), and batch reproducibility must be proved. Safety needs exposure assessment: inhalation and skin contact are main routes, and dry nanopowders can form explosive dust clouds. Use containment, local exhaust ventilation, filtration and proper waste disposal. Rules differ by country, so check the current national regulator and material safety data sheet.

keyPoints: Nanomaterials have at least one dimension between about 1 and 100 nm.
For a cube, surface area to volume ratio is 6 ÷ L, so smaller particles have much more surface per unit mass.
The rule of mixtures E_c = fE_f + (1 − f)E_m is an upper bound for aligned continuous fibre composites.
Top-down synthesis reduces size by physical means; bottom-up synthesis builds particles from molecules.
Characterisation needs several techniques because no single method gives size, structure and surface chemistry.
Scale-up and safety require control of agglomeration, dust exposure and reproducible mixing; regulations vary by country.

en.title: Research methods and dissertation in industrial chemistry
en.short: Planning a chemistry research project, analysing data, keeping ethics and writing the thesis.

sections.heading: Literature review
sections.text: Start with a focused question and a search plan: databases, keywords, date limits and inclusion rules. Read primary papers (original experiments) before reviews, and record full references as you go. A literature review is not a list of summaries; it groups findings by theme, compares methods and results, and states the gap your work will fill. Use reliable sources and cite every borrowed idea.

sections.heading: Design and planning
sections.text: Research design links the question to evidence. Define variables (what you change, measure and hold constant), choose controls, replicates and sample size, and decide how results will be analysed before starting. In experimental planning, randomise run order where possible, use blocking to remove known nuisance effects, and run a pilot. A factorial design tests several factors together and can reveal interactions; keep a laboratory notebook and a data management plan.

sections.heading: Data and ethics
sections.text: Statistical analysis begins with descriptive statistics: mean, standard deviation and graphs. Inferential tests estimate whether an effect is likely or due to chance; check their assumptions and report effect sizes and confidence intervals, not only p-values. Example: yields 72, 75 and 78 percent give mean 75, sample standard deviation 3.0 and standard error 3.0 ÷ √3 = 1.73. Ethics covers honest data, no fabrication or plagiarism, consent where people are involved, safe chemical practice, and agreed authorship. Obtain ethics approval where required.

sections.heading: Writing and defence
sections.text: Write the thesis to a clear structure: abstract, introduction, literature review, methods, results, discussion, conclusion and references. Methods must let another chemist repeat the work; results should be presented without interpretation, then discussed against the literature and limitations. In the defence, present the question, method, key results and limitations in plain language, and answer questions honestly.

keyPoints: Turn the research question into a written plan with variables, controls, replicates and a pre-agreed analysis.
Search primary sources systematically and synthesise them by theme to identify the gap.
Randomise and block experimental runs where possible, and keep raw data in a secure notebook or file.
Mean = Σx ÷ n; sample standard deviation s = √(Σ(x − mean)² ÷ (n − 1)); standard error = s ÷ √n.
Report estimates with confidence intervals and check test assumptions; do not rely on p-values alone.
Follow ethics rules on honesty, consent, safety, authorship and data retention, and write and defend the thesis clearly.
